samples.summary: `cliLoginAvailable()` returns true when `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` is unset, so the new CLI-login refusal is bypassed on exactly the cleartext non-loopback deployment it exists to refuse
samples.evidence:
`cliLoginAvailable()` is `if (useSecureCookies() || loopbackCallback()) return true; return callbackHost() === undefined;` (github-auth.guard.ts:72-75). With `COOKIE_SECURE` unset, `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` unset and `NODE_ENV` not `production`, `useSecureCookies()` is false (oauth-state.ts:229-240), `loopbackCallback()` is false, and `callbackHost()` is `undefined` — so the gate returns TRUE and both `CliLoginConfirmMiddleware` (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:121) and `GitHubAuthGuard.assertCliLoginAvailable()` let the CLI login run.

The justification for that exemption ("GitHub's OAuth flow cannot complete without one anyway", lines 65-70) does not hold: `github.strategy.ts:46` passes `callbackURL: configService.get('GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL')!` with no default, and passport-oauth2 simply omits `redirect_uri` when it is undefined, in which case GitHub uses the callback URL registered on the OAuth app. A self-hosted install on `http://wafflebase.example.com` that registered its callback in the GitHub app and never set the env var is therefore a working deployment that the gate waves through.

On that deployment the consent cookie is set without `Secure` and without `__Host-` (confirmCookieOptions() / cliConfirmCookieName() both key off `useSecureCookies()`), so an attacker who can write a cookie for the parent domain (sibling subdomain, on-path over http) plants `wafflebase_cli_confirm=<value they chose>`, computes `cliConfirmToken(<that value>, port, nonce, challenge)` themselves (the HMAC key is the cookie value they planted — cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:104), and navigates the victim to `/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker port>&nonce=…&challenge=…&confirm=<their HMAC>`. The middleware's check at line 147 passes, `__cliConfirmed` is set, the guard mints CLI state, and the callback mints an authorization code for the *victim's* account and redirects it to the attacker's loopback port — full account takeover, which is precisely what the gate was added to prevent.

Fix: treat an absent callback URL as no evidence of *security* rather than evidence of exemption, or require a positive `COOKIE_SECURE=true`/https callback before allowing `?mode=cli`.

samples.summary: The `/launch/<token>` indirection does not close the argv vector it is built for: the token in argv is itself a dereferenceable capability for the authorization URL
samples.evidence:
`armLaunch` (login.ts:826-830) returns `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/launch/<32-byte token>` and that is what goes to `open()` (login.ts:351), i.e. into a child process's argv. The stated threat is "any local user can read (`ps`, `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`)" (login.ts:337-342; docs/design/cli.md "the authorization URL never reaches argv or a log", claiming it "never leaves this process's memory"). But the launch handler (login.ts:654-671) hands the full authorization URL — nonce + PKCE challenge — in a `Location` header to *anyone* who presents the token, with no method check and no other binding. A local user who reads the token out of world-readable `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and GETs it obtains exactly the URL the indirection was supposed to withhold, and can then complete a login in their own browser: the resulting code is minted for the attacker's GitHub account but bound to the victim's challenge and redirected to the victim's `127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?...&state=<victim nonce>`, so the victim's CLI redeems it and saves the attacker's session (session fixation).

What the change does buy is that the theft is now a race (single use, then 410) and therefore detectable rather than silent. That is real but much weaker than the property the code comments and design doc assert; the docs should not claim the secrets stay in-process, and if the argv vector is in scope the launch URL needs a second factor the argv reader does not have (e.g. requiring a loopback source plus a value passed to the browser out of band, or accepting only the first request within a few hundred ms of arming).

samples.summary: `SECRET_PATH_SEGMENTS` asserts it is exhaustive ("There are exactly two"), but `GET /images/:id` is an unauthenticated capability URL whose path segment is the whole access control
searchedFor: grep '@(Get|Post|Put|Patch|Delete)\(' across packages/backend/src (all route decorators enumerated)
read share-link.controller.ts, workspace.controller.ts invite routes, image.controller.ts
read main.ts to confirm no global route prefix
samples.evidence: `image.controller.ts:64` exposes `@Get(':id')` with no guard — the object id alone grants read of the stored image, which may be private document content. `logSafeUrl` redacts only `share-links/*/resolve` and `invites/*/accept` (log-safe-url.ts:92-94) and the comment at lines 63-65 states there are exactly two such routes, so a valid image id is logged verbatim. `customLogLevel` in app.module.ts:52-55 maps `/images` to `debug` on success, but a 5xx (object-store failure) logs at `error` with a *live* id in the line, and the same reasoning the invite/share entries were added under applies. Either add the shape or narrow the exhaustiveness claim in the comment.

samples.summary: `SENSITIVE_PARAMS` omits `confirm` and `challenge`, the two CLI-login values that are protected only by `isAuthPath` succeeding
searchedFor: grep query param names in backend controllers (@Query)
read cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts renderConfirmPage for the emitted param names
samples.evidence: `code`, `state` and `nonce` appear in `SENSITIVE_PARAMS` as well as being covered by the whole-query `/auth` rule, but `confirm` (the CLI consent HMAC, cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:196) and `challenge` (github-auth.guard.ts:113) rely solely on `isAuthPath` matching. `isAuthPath` tests `/^\/auth(?:\/|$)/` on `req.url`'s path (log-safe-url.ts:22), which does not match an absolute-form request target (`GET http://host/auth/github?confirm=…`, which a forward proxy can produce and which Express still routes via `parseurl`). Adding `confirm`/`challenge`/`verifier` to the param list costs nothing and makes the redaction defence-in-depth rather than single-predicate.

samples.summary: README and design doc document an `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET` env var and HKDF-keyed "signing" of the OAuth login bindings; no such code exists and the binding is an unkeyed SHA-256
samples.evidence: `packages/backend/README.md:25` and `docs/design/backend.md:748` describe `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET` as "Key the OAuth login bindings are signed with", HKDF-derived from `JWT_SECRET` by default. Grepping the repository for `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET`, `hkdf` and `bindingSecret` returns no backend source hits; the actual binding is `hashSecret()` = plain `createHash('sha256')` over the cookie secret (oauth-state.ts:266-268), with no key at all. The unkeyed hash is adequate for the double-submit design (the in-code comment at oauth-state.ts:38-41 says so honestly), but the documentation advertises a keyed control and a configuration knob that do nothing, which is how operators end up believing cookie planting is insufficient when `__Host-` is in fact the only thing preventing it.

samples.summary: `login-url.txt` (a pending-login URL carrying nonce + PKCE challenge) is deleted only in the `finally` around `waitForCallback`, so a Ctrl-C'd login leaves it on disk
samples.evidence: `announceLoginUrl` writes the authorization URL to `dirname(getConfigPath())/login-url.txt` mode 0600 (login.ts:152-157) and it is removed only at login.ts:365, inside the `finally` of the `waitForCallback` await. SIGINT — the normal way to abandon a stuck login, and the case this file exists for — terminates the process without running that `finally`, leaving the file behind. Impact is small because the nonce is only useful while the listener runs, and the file is owner-only; but the `rmSync`-then-`writeFileSync` sequence is also a (narrow) symlink TOCTOU when `WAFFLEBASE_CONFIG` points somewhere world-writable such as `/tmp`. A `process.on('SIGINT')` cleanup, or `openSync(file, 'wx', 0o600)`, closes both.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repository: `cliLoginAvailable()` (github-auth.guard.ts:72-75) returns true whenever `callbackHost()` is undefined, and `callbackHost()` (lines 38-46) is undefined both when `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` is unset and when it is unparseable. In that same configuration `isSecureCookie()` (oauth-state.ts:229-240) returns false with `COOKIE_SECURE` unset and `NODE_ENV !== 'production'`, so the consent cookie is set without `Secure` (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:56-68) and without the `__Host-` prefix (oauth-state.ts:62-64) — i.e. exactly the plantable-cookie condition the gate exists to refuse. Both enforcement points key off the one predicate: the middleware skips the confirmation page at cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:121-123 and the guard's `assertCliLoginAvailable()` returns early at github-auth.guard.ts:233, so nothing else stops the flow; `__cliConfirmed` is then set at line 158 and CLI state is minted at github-auth.guard.ts:202-213. The confirm token's HMAC key is the attacker-planted cookie value itself (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:104, compared at 147-151), so the token is forgeable by whoever plants the cookie. The documented justification for the exemption does not hold: github.strategy.ts:46 passes `callbackURL: configService.get('GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL')!` with no default and, unlike the enterprise endpoints spread via `optional()` (lines 12-14, 31-42), an unset value becomes `undefined` and passport-oauth2 simply omits `redirect_uri`, letting GitHub use the app-registered callback — a working deployment. I found no env validation requiring the variable in packages/backend/src, and docs/design/backend.md:755 lists it as not required. No `already-guarded`, `not-present`, or out-of-lane ground applies; this is an auth/CSRF gate bypass in the security lane.

finding.evidence:
`armLaunch` (login.ts:826-830) returns `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/launch/<32-byte token>` and that is what goes to `open()` (login.ts:351), i.e. into a child process's argv. The stated threat is "any local user can read (`ps`, `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`)" (login.ts:337-342; docs/design/cli.md "the authorization URL never reaches argv or a log", claiming it "never leaves this process's memory"). A local user who reads the token out of world-readable `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and GETs it obtains exactly the URL the indirection was supposed to withhold, and can then complete a login in their own browser: the resulting code is minted for the attacker's GitHub account but bound to the victim's challenge and redirected to the victim's `127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?...&state=<victim nonce>`, so the victim's CLI redeems it and saves the attacker's session (session fixation).

What the change does buy is that the theft is now a race (single use, then 410) and therefore detectable rather than silent. That is real but much weaker than the property the code comments and design doc assert; the docs should not claim the secrets stay in-process, and if the argv vector is in scope the launch URL needs a second factor the argv reader does not have (e.g. requiring a loopback source plus a value passed to the browser out of band, or accepting only the first request within a few hundred ms of arming).

verdict.reason: Every element of the finding is present as described. armLaunch (login.ts:826-830) returns http://127.0.0.1:<port>/launch/<32-byte token>, which is passed to deps.openBrowser at login.ts:351 and thence to open(url) (login.ts:118-126), placing the token in a child process's argv — the world-readable vector the code's own comment names at login.ts:337-342. The launch handler (login.ts:654-671) is an unbound bearer-capability dereference: it compares only the token (nonceMatches, login.ts:656) and then returns the complete authorization URL, containing the nonce and PKCE challenge (built at login.ts:344), in a 302 Location header. There is no method check there, unlike /callback which enforces GET at login.ts:703-706, and no source or timing binding. The chain completes: an attacker who reads the token from /proc/<pid>/cmdline, dereferences it, and completes consent under the victim's nonce and challenge causes the backend to redirect a code minted for the attacker's GitHub account to the victim's 127.0.0.1:<port>/callback with the matching state, which passes the nonce check at login.ts:731 and is redeemed and saved as the victim's session (login.ts:780-783, 398-408) — session fixation. Single use (launchTarget = undefined, login.ts:663) and the 410 page (login.ts:681-689) only reduce this to a pollable race plus a notice the victim may ignore while the CLI waits out CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS (login.ts:516); that is mitigation, not a guard that makes the path unreachable. The asserted stronger property is also genuinely in the tree, not misquoted: docs/design/cli.md:226 states the authorization URL never reaches argv, and packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:88-91 states the URL never leaves this process's memory, while a dereferenceable capability to it does reach argv. In lane (auth/session fixation, sensitive data exposure), reachable, and no named refutation ground applies.

mergedFrom.summary: Session/refresh cookie `Secure` flag is now derived from `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`'s scheme, so a misconfigured `http://` callback on a TLS-fronted deployment silently drops `Secure` from the session token
Session/refresh cookie `Secure` flag silently downgraded from `NODE_ENV` to a derivation of `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`

finding.summary: The session and refresh cookies still carry no `__Host-`/`__Secure-` prefix, so even with `secureCookies()===true` a sibling subdomain can plant `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` — the protection the new comment claims for 'a cookie worth stealing' covers only the `Secure` flag
finding.evidence: `baseCookieOptions` (auth.controller.ts:534-538) returns `{httpOnly, secure, sameSite}` and `setAuthCookies` writes the fixed names `wafflebase_session` / `wafflebase_refresh` (lines 59-60, 484, 492) with no prefix and no `path`. Grep for `__Host-` across packages shows the prefix is applied only in `loginCookieName` (github-auth.guard.ts:238); no session cookie ever gets it. The guard's own reasoning (github-auth.guard.ts:222-232) is that without the prefix any sibling subdomain or anything able to inject a `Set-Cookie` for the registrable domain can write the cookie — applied to the session cookie that is session fixation: an attacker plants their own valid access/refresh token, the victim's browser sends it on every request, and the victim's work lands in the attacker's account. This delta's new comment (lines 527-533) asserts the session cookie's exposure is now handled by `COOKIE_SECURE` + the warning, which addresses only the transport flag, not cookie planting. Pre-existing code, raised because the delta reasons explicitly about this cookie's threat model.

verdict.reason: The session and refresh cookies DO carry the `__Host-` prefix. `oauth-state.ts:62-64` defines `hostPrefixedCookieName()` returning `__Host-${base}` when `isSecureCookie()`, and `oauth-state.ts:86-95` routes `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` through it as `sessionCookieName()`/`refreshCookieName()`. `setAuthCookies` (auth.controller.ts:363-383) writes `res.cookie(sessionCookieName(), ...)` and `res.cookie(refreshCookieName(), ...)` — not fixed bare names. `baseCookieOptions()` (auth.controller.ts:399-414) also includes `path: '/'`, explicitly commented as load-bearing for `__Host-`, contradicting the "no path" claim. The read side is prefixed-only: `jwt.strategy.ts:19` reads solely `cookies[sessionCookieName()]` and `auth.controller.ts:266` reads `cookies[refreshCookieName()]`, so a bare-name cookie planted by a sibling subdomain is never honoured on a Secure deployment; `clearAuthCookies` (auth.controller.ts:349-361) expires both shapes only because deletions carry no credential. Every cited line number and identifier in the finding's evidence (baseCookieOptions at 534-538, names at 59-60/484/492, prefix only in github-auth.guard.ts:238, ACCESS_COOKIE_NAME/REFRESH_COOKIE_NAME) does not correspond to this repository, and the specific threat model the finding says is unaddressed is the documented rationale of oauth-state.ts:66-84.
